{{Short description|Construction in projective geometry}}
In [[mathematics]], an [[algebraic structure]] <math>(R,T)</math> consisting of a non-empty set <math>R</math>  and a ternary mapping <math>T \colon R^3 \to R \,</math> may be called a '''ternary system'''.  A '''planar ternary ring''' (PTR) or '''ternary field''' is a special type of ternary system used by [[Marshall Hall (mathematician)|Marshall Hall]]<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|1943}}</ref> to construct [[projective plane]]s by means of coordinates. A planar ternary ring is not a [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] in the traditional sense, but any [[Field (mathematics)|field]] gives a planar ternary ring where the operation <math>T</math> is defined by <math>T(a,b,c) = ab + c</math>.  Thus, we can think of a planar ternary ring as a generalization of a field where the [[ternary operation]] takes the place of both addition and multiplication.

There is wide variation in the terminology.  Planar ternary rings or ternary fields as defined here have been called by other names in the literature, and the term "planar ternary ring" can mean a variant of the system defined here. The term "ternary ring" often means a planar ternary ring, but it can also simply mean a ternary system.

==Definition==

A '''planar ternary ring''' is a structure <math>(R,T)</math> where <math>R</math> is a set containing at least two distinct elements, called 0 and 1, and <math>T\colon R^3\to R \,</math> is a mapping which satisfies these five axioms:<ref>{{harvnb|Hughes|Piper|1973|loc=p.&nbsp;113, Thm.&nbsp;5.1.}}</ref>
# <math>T(a,0,b)=T(0,a,b)=b,\quad \forall a,b \in R</math>;
# <math>T(1,a,0)=T(a,1,0)=a,\quad \forall a \in R</math>;
# <math>\forall a,b,c,d \in R, a\neq c</math>, there is a unique <math>x\in R</math> such that : <math>T(x,a,b)=T(x,c,d) \,</math>;
# <math>\forall a,b,c \in R</math>, there is a unique <math>x \in R</math>, such that <math>T(a,b,x)=c \,</math>; and
# <math>\forall a,b,c,d \in R, a\neq c</math>, the equations <math>T(a,x,y)=b,T(c,x,y)=d \,</math> have a unique solution <math>(x,y)\in R^2</math>.

When <math>R</math> is finite, the third and fifth axioms are equivalent in the presence of the fourth.<ref>{{harvnb|Hughes|Piper|1973|loc=p. 118, Theorem 5.4}}</ref>

No other pair (0', 1') in <math>R^2</math> can be found such that <math>T</math> still satisfies the first two axioms.

==Binary operations==
===Addition===
Define <math>a\oplus b=T(a,1,b)</math>.<ref>In the literature there are two versions of this definition. This is the form used by {{harvtxt|Hall|1959|loc=p. 355}}, {{harvtxt|Albert|Sandler|1968|loc=p. 50}}, and {{harvtxt|Dembowski|1968|loc=p. 128}}, while <math>a \oplus b = T(1,a,b)</math> is used by {{harvtxt|Hughes|Piper|1973|loc=p. 117}}, {{harvtxt|Pickert|1975|loc=p. 38}}, and {{harvtxt|Stevenson|1972|loc=p. 274}}. The difference comes from the alternative ways these authors coordinatize the plane.</ref> The structure <math>(R,\oplus)</math> is a [[Loop (algebra)|loop]] with [[identity element]] 0.

===Multiplication===
Define <math>a\otimes b=T(a,b,0)</math>. The set <math>R_{0} = R \setminus \{0\} \,</math> is closed under this multiplication.  The structure <math>(R_{0},\otimes)</math> is also a loop, with identity element 1.

===Linear PTR===
A planar ternary ring <math>(R,T)</math> is said to be ''linear'' if <math>T(a,b,c)=(a\otimes b)\oplus c,\quad \forall a,b,c \in R</math>.
For example, the planar ternary ring associated to a [[quasifield]] is (by construction) linear.

==Connection with projective planes==
[[File:Projective_Plane_Coordinates.svg |thumb|Coordinates of a projective plane to establish a planar ternary ring]]

Given a planar ternary ring <math>(R,T)</math>, one can construct a [[projective plane]] with point set ''P'' and line set ''L'' as follows:<ref>R. H. Bruck, ''Recent Advances in the Foundations of Euclidean Plane Geometry'', The American Mathematical Monthly, vol. 66, pp. 2-17 (1955) Appendix I.</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Hall|1943|loc=p.247 Theorem 5.4}}</ref>  (Note that <math>\infty</math> is an extra symbol not in <math>R</math>.)

Let
* <math>P=\{(a,b)|a,b\in R\}\cup \{(a)|a \in R \}\cup \{(\infty)\}</math>, and 
* <math>L=\{[a,b]|a,b \in R\}\cup\{[a]|a \in R \}\cup \{[\infty]\}</math>.

Then define, <math>\forall a,b,c,d \in R</math>, the [[incidence relation]] <math>I</math> in this way:
:<math>((a,b),[c,d])\in I \Longleftrightarrow T(a,c,d)=b</math>
:<math>((a,b),[c])\in I \Longleftrightarrow a=c</math>
:<math> ((a,b),[\infty])\notin I</math>
:<math>((a), [c,d])\in I \Longleftrightarrow a=c</math>
:<math>((a), [c])\notin I</math>
:<math>((a),[\infty])\in I</math>
:<math>((\infty),[c,d])\notin I</math>
:<math>((\infty),[a])\in I</math>
:<math>((\infty),[\infty])\in I</math>

Every projective plane can be constructed in this way, starting with an appropriate planar ternary ring.  However, two nonisomorphic planar ternary rings can lead to the construction of [[Isomorphism|isomorphic]] projective planes.

Conversely, given any projective plane π, by choosing four points, labelled ''o'', ''e'', ''u'', and ''v'', no three of which lie on the same line, coordinates can be introduced in π so that these special points are given the coordinates: ''o'' = (0,0), ''e'' = (1,1), ''v'' = (<math>\infty</math>) and ''u'' = (0).<ref>This can be done in several ways. A short description of the method used by {{harvtxt|Hall|1943}} can be found in {{harvtxt|Dembowski|1968|loc=p. 127}}.</ref> The ternary operation is now defined on the coordinate symbols (except <math>\infty</math>) by ''y'' = T(''x'',''a'',''b'') if and only if the point (''x'',''y'') lies on the line which joins (''a'') with (0,''b''). The axioms defining a projective plane are used to show that this gives a planar ternary ring. 

Linearity of the PTR is equivalent to a geometric condition holding in the associated projective plane.<ref>{{harvnb|Dembowski|1968|loc=p. 129}}</ref>

===Intuition===
The algebraic structure of a [[planar ternary ring]] (PTR) corresponds directly to the coordinates of an [[Affine plane (incidence geometry)|affine plane]]. While PTRs are often used to classify projective planes, the connection is best understood by examining the affine case first.

In [[affine geometry]], points are described using [[Cartesian coordinates]]. This method is applicable even in [[non-Desarguesian plane|non-Desarguesian geometries]]; in such contexts, the coordinate components always obey the structure of a PTR. By contrast, the [[homogeneous coordinates]] typically used in [[projective geometry]] are unavailable in [[non-Desarguesian geometry|non-Desarguesian]] contexts. Thus, the simplest [[analytic geometry|analytic]] way to construct a projective plane in this context is to start with an affine plane and extend it by adding a "[[line at infinity]]".

In an affine plane, the algebraic representation of lines depends on the geometry:
* In a Desarguesian plane, lines follow the standard [[slope-intercept form]] <math>y = mx + c</math>.
* In a non-Desarguesian plane, this representation extends through the ternary operation of a PTR, expressed as <math>y = T(x, m, c)</math>.
In both cases, lines parallel to the y-axis are expressed as <math>x = c</math>.

We can now derive the [[analytic geometry|analytic]] representation of a general projective plane, denoted as <math>R\mathbb{P}^2</math>. This involves expanding the affine plane (<math>R^2</math>) by including the line at infinity. Formally, the projective plane is described as:
:<math>R\mathbb{P}^2 := R^2 \cup R\mathbb{P}^1</math>
Where <math>R^2</math> represents the affine plane (all finite points in Cartesian coordinates) and <math>R\mathbb{P}^1</math> denotes the line at infinity.

To fully define the geometry, the line at infinity is further decomposed:
:<math>R\mathbb{P}^1 := R^1 \cup R \mathbb{P}^0</math>
Here, <math>R^1</math> is an affine line with its own Cartesian coordinate system, and <math>R \mathbb{P}^0</math> consists of a single point (often represented as <math>\infty</math>) not lying on that affine line.

==Related algebraic structures==
PTR's which satisfy additional algebraic conditions are given other names. These names are not uniformly applied in the literature. The following listing of names and properties is taken from {{harvtxt|Dembowski|1968|loc=p. 129}}.
 
A linear PTR whose additive loop is [[Associative property|associative]] (and thus a [[Group (mathematics)|group ]]), is called a '''cartesian group'''. In a cartesian group, the mappings

<math>x \longrightarrow -x \otimes a + x \otimes b </math>, and
<math>x \longrightarrow a \otimes x - b \otimes x </math>

must be permutations whenever <math>a \neq b</math>. Since cartesian groups are groups under addition, we revert to using a simple "+" for the additive operation.

A [[quasifield]] is a cartesian group satisfying the right distributive law:
<math> (x+y) \otimes z = x \otimes z + y \otimes z </math>.
Addition in any quasifield is [[Commutative property|commutative]].

A [[semifield]] is a quasifield which also satisfies the left distributive law:
<math> x \otimes (y + z) = x \otimes y + x \otimes z.</math>

A '''planar [[Near-field (mathematics)|nearfield]]''' is a quasifield whose multiplicative loop is associative (and hence a group). Not all nearfields are planar nearfields.
